issue.title: [chrony][BMC] System clock never converges after reboot/power-cycle on RTC-less BMC platforms (makestep is disabled)

failure.body:
## Describe the bug

On SONiC BMC platforms without a battery-backed/persistent RTC (e.g. Aspeed AST2700-based BMC cards), the system clock comes up at a stale time after every boot and **never converges to the correct time**, even with NTP configured. `chronyc tracking` permanently reports `Leap status: Not synchronised`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Deploy a SONiC BMC image on an Aspeed AST2700-based BMC (no persistent RTC).
2. Reboot — and in particular **power-cycle** — the BMC.
3. Log in and run `date` and `chronyc tracking`.

## Expected behavior

After boot (and once an NTP source is reachable), the system clock converges to the correct time within seconds.

## Actual behavior

The clock comes up weeks/months in the past and never corrects:

```
Reference ID    : 00000000 ()
Stratum         : 0
Ref time (UTC)  : Thu Jan 01 <IPV6> 1970
Leap status     : Not synchronised
```

## Root cause analysis

**1. No persistent RTC on the BMC.** The on-SoC RTC is not battery-backed, so it resets on every power cycle. Kernel log at each boot:

```
aspeed-rtc 12c0f000.rtc: setting system clock to 1970-01-01T01:04:44 UTC (3884)
```

`systemd` then only advances the clock as far as its build epoch, so userspace sees a time pinned near the **image build date** (the offset from real time grows with image age).

**2. `makestep` is disabled in the shared chrony template** — `files/image_config/chrony/chrony.conf.j2`:

```jinja
# Disabled because we don't want chrony to do any clock steps; it should only slew
#makestep 1 3
```

This is intentional: the system clock is meant to only *slew* and never *step*, relying on a persistent RTC to provide correct time at boot. That is appropriate for switches but breaks on an RTC-less BMC — the boot-time offset is large, and chrony's default maximum slew rate (~8.3%, ≈83333 ppm) means correcting an offset of *N* seconds takes ≈ 12·*N* seconds, so a multi-week offset effectively never converges and each reboot resets it.

Background on why stepping is disabled (slew-only by design): see References.

> Note: a reachable, trustworthy NTP source is also required — `chrony` can only step/slew to a time it actually receives. That part is deployment-specific and separate from this issue.

## References

- HLD — SONiC Migration to Chrony: https://github.com/sonic-net/SONiC/blob/master/doc/ntp/migration-to-chrony.md
- HLD tracking issue: sonic-net/SONiC#1852
- ntpd → chrony PR: #20497
- Config template: `files/image_config/chrony/chrony.conf.j2`

resolution.title: Add a service to save the epoch frequently
resolution.description:
#### Why I did it

For devices that may not have a reliable hardware clock (or don't have a hardware clock at all), systemd has a feature where it will update the system time with a more reasonable time if it sees that the time is wildly off or known to be incorrect. One of the sources of a reasonable time is an epoch file, at `/usr/lib/clock-epoch`. If the modification
time of the epoch file is greater than the system time, then it will update the system time to the modification time of the epoch file.

Fixes #27908

##### Work item tracking
- Microsoft ADO **(number only)**:

#### How I did it

Take advantage of this by writing an epoch file daily, so that if the device goes for a reboot (planned or unplanned), the system time is reasonably close. Also bind-mount that file from `/host` into `/usr/lib/clock-epoch`, so that it can be used across images.

#### How to verify it

Create the epoch file, set the time back to far before the epoch timestamp, reboot, and verify that the time from the epoch file is used.
